opus-5.5.text:
I don't think AGI is really a destination in the sense of a single moment where you plant a flag and say, "We're here." It's more like a direction, or maybe a continuum. Every time the models get stronger, our definition of what counts as "general" shifts a little, because things that seemed like magic two years ago start to feel ordinary. So if you try to define AGI as one benchmark or one test, I think you'll always be either too early or too late in declaring it.

The way I prefer to think about it is in terms of capability and impact. Can the system take on longer and more complex tasks with less human supervision? Can it reason, use tools, write and run code, and correct its own mistakes over many steps? And beyond the technical side, is it actually changing how people work and how much value gets created in society? I think those are more meaningful signals than any single exam score.

There's also a philosophical layer. Intelligence isn't a fixed quantity you fill up to 100%. It's open-ended. Even humans don't have a ceiling on what we can learn or discover. So in some sense the more interesting goal is not "reaching AGI" but building systems that can keep improving and keep expanding the frontier of what we know, including in science, mathematics, and things we haven't thought of yet.

So if you push me for an answer: I think we'll look back and realize we crossed many important thresholds gradually, and at some point people will just agree that the label fits. But for those of us building it, the more practical question is always the next step. What's the next capability that's missing, and how do we get there? That's what keeps the work concrete.

r001.rationale: It describes AGI as a direction or continuum, with thresholds crossed gradually rather than a single definitive arrival point.

r002.rationale: It discusses societal impact as a signal of progress, but does not suggest that impact will unfold on a longer timescale than technological development.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think AGI is a destination you reach and then plant a flag on. The way I think about it, it's more of a process than a point. If you ask ten people what AGI is, you'll get ten definitions, and most of them are moving targets. Five years ago, if you showed someone a model that could write code, pass the bar exam, and hold a coherent conversation across any domain, many would have said that's AGI. Now we have that, and nobody is satisfied. The goalposts move, and I actually think that's healthy, because it reflects that intelligence isn't a single threshold.

So I'd rather frame it as a curve. What matters is the slope: how fast is capability going up, and is the mechanism behind that growth still scaling? At Moonshot our view has been that the key variable is long-context and the ability to turn more and more of the world into something the model can actually use, whether that's reading an entire codebase, a company's full history, or a user's memory over years. If you can keep increasing the amount of useful information the model can absorb and act on, and keep increasing the length of the tasks it can complete autonomously, then at some point the question "have we reached AGI" stops being interesting. The system is just doing more and more of the work.

The honest version is: I don't think anyone gets to claim it. There won't be a press release that settles it. It'll be something people recognize in hindsight, the way we recognize the internet era started without any one day being the day. What a lab can claim is narrower and more useful: we can show that on a specific class of tasks, with a specific time horizon, the model is reliably doing what a competent person would do. Keep expanding that class and that horizon. That's the job. Whether you call the end state AGI is a naming question, and naming questions are the least important part.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says AGI is a process or curve, not a destination with a definitive point of arrival.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses changing definitions and recognizing AGI in hindsight, but does not compare the timescale of societal impact with the pace of technological development.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s difficult to treat AGI as a destination where you cross a line and say, “We’ve arrived.” First, you have to define what that line means. Is it performing well on a set of benchmarks? Doing most tasks a human can do? Or being able to learn and solve unfamiliar problems independently? Those are quite different standards.

I’d focus more on what the system can actually do, how reliably it does it, and how much human guidance it needs. If it succeeds at a difficult task but requires someone to keep correcting it, that’s different from being able to handle the whole process independently.

So I see AGI more as a direction for research than a label you claim. The meaningful progress is in expanding the range of problems these systems can solve and making those capabilities useful in practice.

r001.rationale: It describes AGI as a direction for research rather than a label or destination where one can declare arrival.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the timescale of AGI’s societal impact with the pace of technological development.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s hard to treat AGI as a single destination where you cross a line and say, “We’ve arrived.” The definition changes as systems become more capable. Something that looked like a strong test of intelligence a few years ago can become routine, and then we ask for something more.

So I would focus on concrete capabilities. Can the system learn something new, generalize to unfamiliar situations, and complete difficult tasks reliably with less human guidance? Where does it still fail? Those questions are more useful than the label. Even if someone declares that they’ve reached AGI, there will still be a lot of work to do.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AGI is hard to treat as a destination with a clear arrival point and that the definition shifts as systems improve.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses changing capabilities and ongoing work, but does not compare the timescale of AGI’s societal impact with the pace of technological development.
